items.title: L’Iran ha quasi esaurito il petrolio della “flotta fantasma”
items.summary: Cioè quello caricato sulle petroliere prima del blocco navale statunitense, che era una fonte essenziale di ricavi per il regime
items.content:
L’Iran ha quasi esaurito le scorte di petrolio che era riuscito a caricare sulla flotta di petroliere prima del blocco navale statunitense ai suoi porti, che è in atto da aprile e aveva avuto una breve interruzione in estate durante i negoziati infruttuosi tra il regime iraniano e l’amministrazione statunitense di Donald Trump.

Si tratta di petroliere della cosiddetta “ flotta fantasma ”, vecchie imbarcazioni usate per eludere le sanzioni internazionali, che sono già oltre lo stretto di Hormuz. Per il regime iraniano è un problema perché i proventi dei carichi, venduti anzitutto alla Cina , sono essenziali per l’economia nazionale, messa sempre peggio proprio a causa del blocco. Venerdì il comando delle forze statunitensi in Medio Oriente ha sostenuto che il blocco abbia impedito all’Iran ricavi per 25 miliardi di dollari dalle vendite di petrolio.

Di solito i carichi vengono pagati nel giro di due mesi dalla consegna, quindi per un po’ di tempo il regime continuerà a ricevere i versamenti in valuta straniera di cui ha bisogno. Però adesso, di fatto per la prima volta dall’inizio della guerra lo scorso febbraio, l’Iran sta rimanendo senza petrolio in mare.

Secondo la società specializzata Kpler, all’inizio di ottobre rimaneva sulle petroliere meno di 1 milione di barili di petrolio, contro i 135 milioni di barili all’inizio della guerra. Tra giugno e luglio, con la sospensione del blocco navale, il regime aveva cercato di concentrare le partenze di petroliere, ma anche questi carichi si sono ormai esauriti.

Storicamente l’Iran ha usato le petroliere come una specie di riserva galleggiante, anche perché durante il blocco statunitense aveva saturato i depositi a terra. Dopo la partenza, le petroliere della “flotta fantasma” stazionano al largo delle coste di Malaysia e Singapore. Da lì i carichi, per essere meno rintracciabili, vengono trasferiti su altre petroliere che li portano a destinazione in Cina.

I proventi delle vendite di petrolio sono la principale fonte di valuta straniera per il governo iraniano e coprono fino al 40 per cento del bilancio statale. Le alternative via terra finora non sono state sufficienti. Al contrario, le esportazioni di petrolio degli altri paesi del Golfo Persico, sotto la guida degli Stati Uniti attraverso Hormuz o lungo percorsi alternativi, da poco hanno superato i livelli di prima della guerra.

items.title: Anatomy of a generation’s rage: why Italy’s teenagers are taking to the streets
items.summary: From looting in Milan to student protests in Rome: who are the teenagers taking to the streets? Like their peers across Europe, they are driven by anger, but Italy’s unrest has a history stretching back decades.
items.content:
ROME – It has been called the children’s war, the fury of the TikTok generation, the revolt of those who cannot afford to buy the world, so they set about smashing it instead. A wave of attacks, looting, demonstrations and strikes is sweeping Italy from north to south in this autumn of discontent. It recalls the Hot Autumn of 1969, when a great wave of strikes brought together workers in Italy’s major factories and protesting students.

Today’s unrest unites young Italians with their counterparts in France, Spain and Albania. It is a collective outpouring of anger at the cost of living, unaffordable rents, crumbling schools and insecure jobs. But it is also, quite simply, anger for anger’s sake.

Genuine grievances in a country growing ever poorer, with an ever-widening gulf between social classes, are becoming entangled with something else. More than five million people in Italy live in absolute poverty, including one million children. Yet alongside those protesting against these inequalities is a growing army of teenagers, some as young as 12 or 13, who descend on city centres from the outer suburbs to join in street battles and grab goods, often luxury items, that they cannot afford and may never be able to buy.

That is why it is so difficult today to make sense of the anatomy of this protest movement. It differs not only between Rome and Milan, Turin and Naples, but even within individual cities.

Take Milan, where images of Piazza del Duomo being turned into a battleground by gangs of very young first- and second-generation Italians — including, but by no means limited to, groups disparagingly labelled maranza — have circulated around the world in recent days.

Responding to calls spread on Instagram, TikTok and Telegram to “come on, let’s smash everything up”, crowds of teenagers wearing trap-style hoodies and balaclavas poured into the heart of Milan from the suburbs.

They looted supermarkets and stores belonging to Decathlon, Nike and Levi’s, stealing trainers, jeans and designer sweatshirts. Armed with clubs and setting rubbish bins alight, they fought pitched battles with the police — or the “cops”, as they call them.

Smashing things up for the sake of it, causing chaos for chaos’s sake, often livestreaming their acts of vandalism on social media.

No politics, no slogans, just raw anger. Or perhaps simply boredom, and the surreal appeal of doing something different on a Saturday afternoon.

But it would be a mistake to focus solely on these teenage looters, because Italy’s protest movement takes many different forms and operates on many levels.

In simple terms, it brings together legitimate demands — starting with those of students and the thousands of families who have run out of money to live on by the third week of the month — with violence for violence’s sake, an existential eruption from a social-media generation that has grown accustomed to carrying knives in its pockets. (The number of minors arrested for illegally carrying weapons in Italy has risen by 455% in ten years.)

And the frustration is not confined to the young. Consider the revolt by lorry drivers against the prohibitive cost of petrol and diesel, which is disrupting the supply of goods across the country, leaving supermarkets in entire regions with depressingly empty shelves.

“We’ve got panettone on the shelves, but we’re running out of meat and milk,” one distressed shop assistant reported.

It is anger reminiscent of France’s Yellow Vest movement, and farmers and livestock breeders are now threatening to join the lorry drivers.

But who is organising these demonstrations, which increasingly descend into street battles?

Among the bewildering array of groups and acronyms that appear and disappear on social media, one name currently stands out: Italiainpiazza17. The number 17 referred to 17 October, and the group will become Italiainpiazza24 for the next demonstration, scheduled for 24 October.

It is a newly formed network with no leaders or political representatives, which emerged on Instagram and Telegram as French students were occupying one secondary school after another, as well as streets, squares and universities, even reaching the entrance to the Louvre.

Its founding manifesto declares that Italiainpiazza is non-partisan and peaceful, invoking Article 17 of the Italian Constitution: “Citizens have the right to assemble peacefully and unarmed.”

The movement says it was created to protest against the cost of living, lack of access to healthcare, poverty wages, underfunded schools and universities that offer little prospect of a future.

In other words, it is a banner capable of channelling and bringing together the full range of social grievances felt by Generation Z and, ultimately, by their parents too.

But it is also such a loosely defined movement that its umbrella attracts not only individuals and groups who legitimately want to protest without joining political parties or trade unions, but also populists and provocateurs of every kind.

They range from anti-vaccine campaigners to far-right extremists such as Andrea Ballarati, a well-known racist agitator who has previously been investigated and has extensive connections with European supremacist and remigration parties and movements. He was quick to launch the slogan “We’ll take to the streets too” on Telegram.

So today, as during every great wave of protest, organised groups of provocateurs are infiltrating demonstrations, using chaos and violence to undermine the legitimacy and strength of the demands being made.

It happened in the 1970s, with the strategy of tension that began with the Piazza Fontana bombing in 1969, an attempt to extinguish the spirit of change unleashed by the youth protests of 1968. It failed to do so.

But a decade of bombings, followed by the Years of Lead, when the Red Brigades brought further bloodshed, left Italy mourning hundreds of dead.

It would be wrong, however, to take the young casseurs who devastated Milan as the defining symbol of what is happening in Italy.

To understand the heart of the student movement, we need to look instead to Rome and Turin.

In the capital, where the protests have so far avoided violence apart from firecrackers thrown at the Education Ministry, dozens of secondary schools have been occupied in just a few days, in solidarity with the French protests.

At the centre of the movement is the despair of a generation that feels it has been robbed of its future: dilapidated schools, exorbitant textbook prices, student accommodation that is either unavailable or privately run, while the government triples spending on armaments.

It is no coincidence that the movement has named itself Generazione Fuoriclasse, a play on words suggesting both a generation left outside the classroom and one that is a class apart.

Angela Verreccia, coordinator of the Rete degli Studenti Medi, the national secondary school students’ network, explains:

“With Generazione Fuoriclasse, we want to build a permanent protest movement against the rising cost of education, the cost of living and the lack of protections. The conditions in which we are too often forced to study are not individual problems. They are political and collective issues that demand structural solutions.”

Meanwhile, the tent encampments set up by university students in Rome are expanding by the day, from the avenues of Sapienza University to the square outside the entrance to Parliament, as students protest against soaring rents.

In Turin, meanwhile, a student demonstration that began with the same legitimate demands descended into Milan-style street battles. The ransacking of the Feltrinelli bookshop was particularly shocking.

All this raises the question of whether, starting in Rome, a new Panther movement is beginning to roar among Italian students.

The original Panther was the last great youth movement to emerge in the wake of the protests of 1968, when young people first challenged their parents’ generation and the society it had built.

Then came 1977, when a student movement born in the universities broke with the traditional political parties, particularly the Communist Party, and the trade unions. The most famous episode was the expulsion of CGIL trade union leader Luciano Lama from Rome’s Sapienza University.

The movement embraced new, often creative forms of protest, including those of the Metropolitan Indians, while feminism — the only Italian revolution without deaths or injuries — genuinely and permanently transformed women’s lives.

But the movement, divided between its pacifist wing and the section of the Workers’ Autonomy movement that went on to join the terrorist Red Brigades was eventually extinguished by the descent into armed struggle.

After 1977, it seemed that student protest in Italy had fallen dormant.

Yet in December 1989, the winds of protest began blowing through the universities once again, this time against the university reform proposed by Socialist minister Antonio Ruberti.

At precisely that moment, a black panther escaped from a circus in the countryside around Rome. Despite an enormous hunt to capture it, the animal was never found.

items.title: Inside Daniele Papuli’s studio, where paper becomes art
items.summary: From pristine sheets and printing offcuts to phone books and unwanted old volumes, the Apulian artist—a self-described “sculptographer”—creates elegant sculptures and striking installations out of paper
items.content:
“I like to tempt viewers to step closer to take a better look, kind of like what happens with Lecce Baroque architecture—to spark a sense of wonder: ‘Ah, but it’s paper!’ ”

Daniele Papuli creates objects that could be described by the somewhat overused term art design : one-of-a-kind pieces such as monumental tables, bookcases, or small vases, which he has exhibited for over twenty years at the Dilmos gallery in Milan and which have found their way into private homes in Dubai, Colombia, and across Asia. He also creates site-specific installations, such as Cartomastodonte in Apulia, his home region.

The artwork—installed within the Campo dei Giganti (a rural and artistic regeneration project set among olive trees devastated by the Xylella bacterium)—consists of 35,000 books destined for recycling, laid open and arranged side by side. Over time, the pages have lost their color, turning into a dense, almost fossilized mass that continues to transform.

A few years ago, at the Aragonese Castle of Ischia, a video projected onto a wall showed a landscape of abstract forms created by dipping old receipt paper rolls into blue aniline dye. The imagery seemed to engulf both the surrounding church interior and the viewer.

It is often painstaking work, which Papuli undertakes alone in his studio on the outskirts of Milan, sometimes working through the night. “I come here every day from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.; I don't believe in waiting around for inspiration. The project emerges the moment you start touching, observing, and manipulating the material.”

It is a densely packed space: a palette of paper samples, tunnels of thin strips, towers of reams, and swatches squeezed onto shelves alongside an Afra and Tobia Scarpa leather sofa.

A densely layered, colorful world that also includes earlier works stored in wooden boxes, like props kept backstage at a theater.

A true "lightweight workshop" that he hopes to recreate elsewhere one day, bringing together Papuli’s past, present, and future in a kind of personal museum, open for educational activities and offering space for new ideas.

You describe yourself as a “sculptographer.” What does that mean?

“I coined the term to bring together sculpture and graphic expression—the sculptural quality of the work and the material itself.

"You see, paper naturally generates its own graphic qualities, its own drawing. Sometimes it is so condensed it resembles wood or stone; other times it is layered, and air settles between the sheets. I abandoned classical sculpture—that is to say, the hammer and chisel.”

“Even though I started out with the noble materials of the discipline, like stone and marble, I soon moved on to plaster and plastics. At a certain point, I was searching for something else.

"A trip to Berlin in the early nineties, where I was directing a workshop-seminar for artists, proved pivotal. That was where I saw handmade paper being made for the first time.”

“The oldest technique uses rags. Alternatively, you start with recycled paper or cellulose. It gets shredded, soaked, boiled, and finally blended into a pulp.

"By dipping a mesh-covered frame into the pulp, you obtain a thin layer of paper. I then transfer it onto a table and hang the sheets to dry in the sun.”

So you fell in love with it and started making your own paper.

“I rarely do it nowadays, but a few years after that trip, in 1997, I was given an important commission.”

“Between trial runs and originals, I produced 1,800 handmade sheets for an art book published in a limited run of 300 copies. The volume brought together the poetry of Wisława Szymborska—translated from Polish into Italian—and watercolors by Alina Kalczyńska, a Polish artist and graphic designer who was the wife of publisher Vanni Scheiwiller.

"The entire production took place in Maglie, in Salento, in a completely domestic setting. We experimented with paper shades on Alina and Vanni’s terrace in nearby Otranto, dyeing the paper pulp with tea, coffee, onion skins, and flowers.

"And all of this was done in a rush, right before I left for military service.”

“Right after high school in Maglie, I spent a year studying Set Design at the Brera Academy. But the traumatic impact of the city led me to drop out and enroll at the Academy of Fine Arts in Lecce. Yet as soon as I got back, I realized I’d made a mistake—deep down, I was drawn to Milan.

“In the meantime, back in Salento, I had set up my first workshop in a small room without electricity. There, I carved simple, organic forms inspired by nature out of wood and stone. I returned to Brera to finish my studies.

"I had already begun my research into paper—partly out of financial necessity, mind you, because I couldn't afford premium materials—when one day I arrived by train with my small sculptures packed in a suitcase.”

“I made them using pages from lined notebooks or old books with ivory pages, and each one was kept in its own tiny handmade box that opened like a mini theater.

"One day, walking past the Missoni store, I decided to pitch myself. I went to see them in Sumirago and landed my first major commission.”

“They were about to open their flagship store on Via Verri and entrusted me with designing all the window displays. My sculptures engaged in a dialogue with their garments, which were transformed into kites, trees, and columns.

"That job paved the way for me on Via Montenapoleone; work for Giorgetti, Poliform, Rimadesio, B&B Italia, and Hermès followed.

“The press coverage was extraordinary. I really enjoyed creating window displays, and even though I was taking part in group exhibitions at the time, I preferred storefronts to galleries.”

“Not at all, because to me, what I do is work. An artistic installation—whether in a gallery, at a trade fair, or in the corner of a shop—is always a creative dialogue with space, which ought to be democratic and open. That's precisely what I love about window displays: they aren't intimidating; they seek an active dialogue with the passerby.”

You’ve continued to work across both commercial and artistic contexts, and your portfolio includes objects and furniture. How do you view these pieces?

“To me, every object must first and foremost be an experience: tactile, acoustic, and why not, even olfactory. Ultimately, they are all sculptures: screens, bookcases, consoles, tables, vases. After all, what is a vase if not a sculpture with a hole in it? Today, however, I am mostly drawn to dialogues with other artistic languages.”

“I'm becoming less and less interested in the physical object itself. My work is increasingly moving toward theater, dance, and sound, engaging in a dialogue with the surrounding space. I'm currently working on a contemporary dance performance where the dancers interact with large-scale paper forms and stage sets made entirely of paper.”

items.title: Simone Fontecchio, the Italian NBA star chasing a championship ring
items.summary: Born in Pescara, the 30-year-old plays for the Miami Heat. His value lies in the details: stretching defences, hitting three-pointers, moving without the ball and giving his team an extra weapon when the pressure is on. He also brings a touch of the Italian flair Americans love: warmth, passion, a strong work ethic and discipline
items.content:
New York - There is a particular kind of Italian dream that has survived every generation of basketball players who have crossed the Atlantic. It is not simply about making it to the NBA, earning a contract or hearing a crowd chant your name in the American way.

It is about winning a championship, claiming that coveted ring, slipping it onto your finger and bringing home something no Italian player has won since Marco Belinelli claimed the title with the San Antonio Spurs in 2014.

For Simone Fontecchio, 30, a native of Pescara, that dream has acquired a new address: Miami. And the pursuit of that dream resumed on Wednesday night, when the Heat opened their 2026-27 regular season against the Minnesota Timberwolves at the Kaseya Center in Miami. On Tuesday night the season tipped off with the defending champions, the New York Knicks, losing to the Philadelphia 76ers, led by LeBron James. So, Americans like to say, let’s roll.

As for the star power, the Heat have signed Giannis Antetokounmpo, long regarded as the next LeBron, a dominant force in the Eastern Conference who could put the Heat back in position to contend for an NBA championship in the post-LeBron era.

Since joining the NBA in 2022, Fontecchio - or “Fountechio”, as Americans pronounce his surname - has moved beyond the kid trying to prove he belongs in the league. He has earned his place in the league, survived the adjustments that make the transition from European basketball so difficult and established himself as a reliable perimeter threat.

Averaging 8.5 points per game for the Heat last season, he is back for another year in South Florida, after signing a new contract. He’s ready to compete in an organization where expectations are high and nothing comes easy. And he’ll have to do it in a very demanding city.

The challenge is to turn that opportunity into something bigger.

Fontecchio is not arriving as a franchise savior, nor does he need to be. His value lies in the details: the ability to stretch a defense, punish opponents from beyond the arc, move without the ball and give a team another weapon when the game tightens. And yes, he brings that “Italian flair” Americans love: warmth, work ethic, passion, discipline, a sense of sacrifice and a certain style.

But there is another dimension to Fontecchio’s story, one that cannot be measured in numbers. Fontecchio has basketball in his blood.

His mother, Mali Pomilio, played for the Italian national team and won two European titles with AS Vicenza. His grandfather, Vittorio Pomilio, also wore the national jersey. His father, Daniele, was a hurdler who competed at the highest level, representing Italy at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics. In the Fontecchio family, sport was never merely a profession.

Yet Simone’s path to the NBA was anything but inevitable. He went undrafted in 2017, spent years building his reputation in Europe and finally reached the league with the Utah Jazz in 2022, not exactly a marquee franchise at that time.

This season, Fontecchio’s challenge is not to imitate an American basketball player. No one here wants that. It is to become a trusted teammate while remaining unmistakably himself. His journey echoes those of Belinelli, whose shooting and competitive spirit earned him the affection of American fans, and Vincenzo Esposito, the fearless guard who became one of the pioneers of Italian basketball in the NBA during the Toronto Raptors’ inaugural season in 1995-96.

They arrived in different eras and with very different roles, but both helped make an Italian accent sound a little less foreign in an American locker room. Andrea Bargnani and Danilo Gallinari spent years carving out a career without getting their hands on a championship.

Before them came Dino Meneghin, the Italian Legend, who was selected by the Atlanta Hawks in the 1970 NBA Draft, long before any Italian player made his NBA debut. The story has since become part of basketball folklore: Meneghin did not even learn about his selection until months later. The NBA was still a distant world, almost an abstraction, and the idea of an Italian becoming a meaningful part of it appeared improbable.

But the world has changed since then, and the NBA has changed even more. Fontecchio has the opportunity to take this new Italian tradition one step further. His “paisà” identity is part of the package: the temperament, the humor, the family values and the unpretentious approach that can help a player build relationships far from home.

In the NBA, affection can open a door, but performance keeps it open. The ring, meanwhile, remains the ultimate measure of the dream. In this case, the Italian Dream.

items.title: Cesare Cremonini presents his new album: “It will be the biggest failure in Italian music”
items.summary: The singer-songwriter from Bologna is in London for the launch of Amateur and an intimate gig at Shepherd’s Bush Empire. “Music has never been so boxed in—that’s why I know the algorithm won't get the album.”
items.content:
LONDON – Fail again, fail better. “This album will be my biggest failure. The biggest failure in Italian music.”

Is Cesare Cremonini joking? “No, I mean it,” replies the Bolognese singer-songwriter.

He welcomes us inside Universal's gleaming London headquarters in the now-upmarket district of King’s Cross—once an area where drug dealers, criminals, squatters, and sex workers were a common presence.

The times they are a-changin' . Cremonini has changed, too, at 46. He has titled his latest record Amateur —defined by Roland Barthes as one who loves without fear of their own image, or, as Cesare puts it, “someone who is dead but cannot die, because they are still tethered to life by a passion.

It will be a failure because this record is pure music; it doesn't even have choruses,” he explains. “It’s a door, not a mirror. Today, almost every album is a reflection of itself or its author. Today, the world wants us disconnected. The algorithm only feeds you what you already like. That’s why mirrors have replaced doors. I wanted to take a risk instead.”

The album features a stellar line-up of Italian stars: Salmo on the opening title track; Fabri Fibra on the single Paparazzi , which is already topping the radio charts; alongside Morgan, Elisa, and Malika Ayane—sixteen years after her relationship with Cesare ended.

“Because she is a miracle of detail, and the album needed her sense of femininity.” So why not play it safe and chase commercial success, catchiness, and market trends?

Cremonini explains this during an hour of deep, cultured conversation: “I believe in the karma of music. That is, for those of my generation, the music that outlasts us. Today, however, the algorithm is the karma of music. And I know this album won't be understood by the algorithm. There has never been a moment in history when music was so boxed in. So we should be happy about failures, if they set us free.”

With Amateur , Cremonini swears he feels “like a newcomer all over again. I’m feeling the exact same rush as I did back in 1999 during the (phenomenal) debut of ...Squérez? with Lùnapop: just like then, it’s a leap in the dark. This record,” the tenth of his career, “is like an unplanned child.”

Is he happy now? “I’ve stopped asking myself how I’m doing. It doesn’t matter anymore. What matters is reconnecting records to the imagination, because that is the foundation of empathy. It helps us understand how someone feels when they're lonely and abandoned, or lost at sea in the dead of night. Because culture is invincible. Not even Trump can kill it.”

“And with this record,” Cremonini continues, “I wanted to seal up a bleeding wound in my ego. My long-time manager [Walter Mameli] always kept me ‘grounded’ so I wouldn’t get ahead of myself, much like the coach of tennis legend Andre Agassi. As a result, I became a great racehorse, but one plagued by massive insecurity. Now I’ve changed. I used to feel I had to win ten Wimbledons; now, I’m like a tennis player who simply loves the ball.”

Amateur , a ten-track album set for release on October 23 via Universal, was recorded at “Studio 13,” owned by Blur frontman and singer-songwriter Damon Albarn. “London is vital to me,” Cremonini stresses, “and not just because of David Bowie, Queen, or The Beatles. I came here because I wanted to be a nobody, to step aside and let only the music take centre stage.”

On Tuesday, ahead of his upcoming “Ama-tour” (kicking off in Italy on November 24), Cremonini played an intimate gig at the legendary Shepherd’s Bush Empire, right in the neighbourhood where The Who were formed. An adoring crowd of two thousand fans—including motorcycling legend Valentino Rossi and singer Elisa—cheered on the live preview of the new album, along with covers of Stand by Me and Walk on the Wild Side .

On stage stood gold-plated instruments, alongside a skull named “Sig”—inspired by Sig-mund Freud as well as Damien Hirst. “That skull,” Cremonini concludes, “represents all the passion and dirt you carry with you over the years. Only to let it go, and find your purity again.”

items.title: How Arab parties could hold critical balance of power in Israeli election
items.summary: Disaffection has often driven down turnout among Arab Israelis, but there is a strong push to get rid of the right-wing governing coalition.
items.content:
At rush hour in Nazareth, the largest Arab-majority city in Israel, students are handing out leaflets by the roadside urging motorists to vote in next week's closely fought, general election. Polls indicate that Arab parties could be left holding a critical balance of power.

Disaffection has often driven down past turnout among Arab Israelis - who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel. But this election, there is a strong push to get rid of the most right-wing governing coalition in the country's history - an alliance between veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

"I see it as our duty to bring down this extremist government. They treat us as second-class," says Arkan Badran, 23, who is with the students giving out flyers. "I call on all young men and women to vote for Arab lists, which represent us, because this is our future."

Most opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu and his partners nor the main "Change Bloc", led by centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has a clear path to a parliamentary majority.

If they are right, after the election anti-Netanyahu parties wanting to form a governing coalition would either have to go back on pledges not to work with the prime minister or make a deal with Arab-majority lists.

A major sticking point is that Eisenkot has so far ruled out forming a government with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values.

Israel's politics and society have been changed by the deadly, unprecedented Hamas-led assault on the country on 7 October 2023, and subsequent war in Gaza. There is increased mistrust of and hostility towards the country's Arab minority.

"After October 7, we were treated as enemies of this country," says Suha Salman Mousa of the Mossawa Centre in Nazareth, which advocates for equal rights for Arab citizens. "There was shrinking space for freedom of speech. There were major arrests, there was also firing of people from their workplaces because they put something on social media or they went out against the war on Gaza."

Salman Mousa accuses ministers of "systematic discrimination and incitement" against Arab Israelis. Civil society groups say they have disproportionately cut budgets for Arab communities. The government says reductions are needed to fund wartime defence and security spending.

There have also been politicised campaigns against Arab physicians working in Israeli hospitals and racially motivated attacks on Arab bus drivers by Jewish Israelis.

Some electioneering has sought to capitalise by deepening social divisions. The far-right Finance Minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has vowed to "Judaise" parts of the northern Galilee and southern Negev regions where most Arabs live, likening this to expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank.

How do Israel's elections work and who are the main contenders?

The majority of Arab Israelis are descendants of Palestinians who remained within what became Israel during the war that surrounded the creation of the state in 1948, when hundreds of thousands were forced from or fled their homes. Israel's current government often frames them as a threat to the state's Jewish identity. Recently, the prime minister has claimed that his rivals plan to team up with Arabs and form a "dangerous government".

To make this point, his campaign has put up billboards, including one at a road junction at the main entrance to Nazareth. They suggest a choice between: "Right or Palestine" - with pictures of main opposition figures, including right-wingers, depicted as representing the latter not the former. The Netanyahu campaign has also used AI-generated videos to present his opponents embracing Arab leaders.

At Radio Nas, a popular Arabic-language station in Nazareth, I meet news anchor Mohammed Magadli, who is also an analyst for Israel's Channel 12. His father, Raleb Magadli, served as Israel's first Muslim minister between 2007 and 2009, representing the Labour party.

I ask the younger Magadli what he makes of Change Bloc leaders refusing to join forces with Arab parties.

"In a word it's racism. But if we're trying to explain why, it's because of the political interests of Benjamin Netanyahu," he says. "He's trying all the time to pull the legitimacy of the Arab parties - because they're Arab, because they're Palestinian. This is affecting the majority of the Jewish parties in Israel."

Polls this week have suggested that both Eisenkot's bloc and Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc could each win around 50 seats of the 120 in Israel's parliament while 13 or 14 seats in total could go to Arab-majority groupings.

These are the Joint Arab List, a coalition of Hadash, Balad and Taal, and the smaller United Arab List, an Islamist party headed by politician Mansour Abbas.

While Abbas's party was originally created as part of the Islamic Movement in Israel - which has socially conservative values - he has become known for joining with Jewish partners. He prioritises solving the problems of Arab Israelis and speaks relatively little of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.

Abbas has had a taste of power. In 2021, he became a minister in a previous, short-lived Israeli government led by Naftali Bennett - now a right-wing member of Eisenkot's bloc.

For this election, he has taken the surprise step of giving the number two position on his slate to a Jewish former police official and centrist member of parliament, Yoav Segalovitz. Abbas believes Eisenkot and others will be more open to an alliance with his party after the election and insists he wants to join the next government.

"We've reached the conclusion that parliamentary representation is not enough to serve Arab society. We decided to take responsibility, to become part of the solution to our problems and to offer hope to both Arabs and Jews," he tells me.

"That's why our approach has been driven by a desire to reach a position of influence, not merely representation."

Meanwhile, the Joint List - which is made up of secular parties and advocates for equal rights for Arab Israelis, an end to Israeli military occupation of Palestinian territories, and a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict - aims to wield a position of influence within the opposition.

It talks of providing an electoral "safety net" to those who could replace the Netanyahu government, in return for support on important policies.

A main issue in this election for Arab Israelis is rampant gang crime.

In September, a poll by the Israel Democracy Institute think tank found that this was the most important factor for 53.5% of Arab citizens when deciding which party to vote for.

Murders within the community reached a record high of 252 last year – about five times higher than the number of Jewish Israelis who were killed, according to the Abraham Initiatives, a Jewish-Arab organisation that promotes coexistence.

In Jaffa, a mixed Arab-Jewish neighbourhood which is now joined to Tel Aviv, Ziad Samouni shows me where his son, Hussein, was shot dead by two gunmen on a motorcycle near his home last November.

No arrests have been made in his case. With a low percentage of cases solved, Arab-Israelis accuse the government of inaction.

"It seems they're interested in making sure we reach a situation where the killer is never caught, allowing Arabs in Arab society to keep killing one another," says Samouni, who is now part of a support group, Israeli-Palestinian Bereaved Families for Peace.

The Israeli police told the BBC its investigation into Hussein's murder remained active, adding that it took "every case of violence and crime with the utmost seriousness."

"As a father who's lost a son, of course, I want this bloodshed to end," Samouni tells me. "I wish every Arab citizen who believes there needs to be a change sees that this is a time to go to vote."

This month, Israel's Supreme Court overruled a decision by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify the United Arab List and the Joint List as well as two of their members.

The committee, which is dominated by the governing coalition, argued that they broke a law banning candidates who deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish state. The parties and their representatives strongly denied it.

With just days to go before voting, back in Nazareth, some motorists display flags for their preferred party on their cars.

The stakes are high in this election: Arab citizens could yet decide who wields power in Israel, and they also see this vote as key to their own future in the country.

Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters

items.title: Gli studenti protestano anche in Grecia
items.summary: Mercoledì sono scesi in piazza in modo pacifico in una decina di città, chiedendo le stesse cose di italiani e francesi
items.content:
Mercoledì in una decina di città greche gli studenti delle scuole superiori e delle università si sono uniti al movimento di protesta che nelle ultime settimane ha attraversato Francia e Italia. Le rivendicazioni degli studenti greci sono simili a quelle dei compagni italiani e francesi: chiedono più investimenti nella scuola e misure per contrastare l’aumento del costo della vita e degli affitti. In Grecia gli insegnanti di elementari e superiori si sono uniti alle proteste, scioperando per 24 ore.

Le proteste sono state pacifiche e non ci sono stati scontri paragonabili a quelli dei primi giorni in Francia o dello scorso fine settimana in Italia , anche se alcuni commercianti si erano premurati di chiudere il negozio e abbassare le saracinesche. Ad Atene a corteo finito un gruppo di ragazzi ha lanciato pietre e bottiglie contro gli agenti in tenuta antisommossa, che hanno risposto con lacrimogeni, ma la stessa polizia ha detto che è stato un episodio isolato. Sono state fermate 25 persone.

Ad Atene la protesta era iniziata il giorno prima, quando gli studenti si erano accampati con alcune tende davanti al parlamento in piazza Syntagma. Mercoledì 18 scuole sulle 30 della città risultavano occupate.

Per far comprendere le istanze degli studenti, il coordinamento studentesco della città ha preso a esempio un paio di episodi che evidenziano lo stato decadente delle infrastrutture scolastiche: solo nei giorni scorsi un pezzo di intonaco è caduto dal soffitto e ha ferito uno studente a Salonicco, e una fuga di gas ha causato l’evacuazione di 4mila studenti ad Atene, tra gli altri.

«Non permetteremo che le nostre scuole diventino le nuove “Tempi”» si legge nel comunicato. Tempi è un riferimento al gravissimo incidente ferroviario che nel 2023 causò la morte di 57 persone, e che molti in Grecia attribuiscono ai problemi strutturali della rete ferroviaria e alla corruzione del governo (anche se a causarlo fu un errore umano).

Gli studenti delle superiori rivendicano il diritto a studiare in edifici sicuri, a non avere cattedre vuote e l’azzeramento dell’IVA sul cibo venduto nelle scuole, tra le altre cose. Quelli delle università chiedono invece maggiori sussidi per l’affitto (ora di 120 euro al mese) e più posti negli studentati, per contrastare il carovita. Gli insegnanti che si sono uniti chiedono l’aumento della spesa per l’istruzione al 5 per cento del PIL e il ripristino di tredicesima e quattrodicesima.

Il governo greco, di centrodestra, ha risposto con scetticismo ai metodi delle proteste. La ministra dell’Istruzione Sofia Zacharachi ha detto di non credere nelle scuole chiuse e che l’occupazione sia una soluzione, «ma avete ragione sugli edifici e sui bisogni». Il primo ministro Kyriakos Mitsotakis invece aveva sostenuto che «il paese non tornerà mai all’epoca dei grandi disordini sociali», riferendosi alle proteste che dopo la crisi finanziaria del 2007-2008 e le misure di austerità imposte dall’Europa alla Grecia investirono tutto il paese.

Le proteste degli studenti aumentano la pressione sul governo di Mitsotakis, che sta attraversando un momento complicato. È in carica dal 2019 ma i suoi consensi sono scesi sotto al 30 per cento, principalmente a causa del carovita e delle accuse di corruzione. Le prossime elezioni sono in programma per il 2027, e Mitsotakis ha escluso che si possa andare a elezioni anticipate.

items.title: L’azienda di e-commerce eBay eliminerà altri mille posti di lavoro, circa il 9 per cento del totale
items.content:
Martedì la piattaforma di e-commerce eBay ha comunicato al proprio staff che eliminerà altri mille posti di lavoro, pari a circa il 9 per cento del totale. Alla fine del 2025 l’azienda aveva circa 12.300 dipendenti, e a febbraio aveva già annunciato l’eliminazione di 800 posti. Un portavoce ha detto che la misura è pensata perché eBay continui a operare da una «posizione di forza», in linea con le proprie «priorità strategiche».

Dopo alcuni anni complicati, dall’anno scorso eBay è tornata a crescere, e tra le altre cose a inizio 2026 ha acquisito Depop, una piattaforma online per la compravendita di abbigliamento di seconda mano prima controllata dal gruppo Etsy. Lo scorso maggio il suo consiglio di amministrazione aveva rifiutato una proposta di acquisto ambiziosa da parte della catena di negozi di videogiochi GameStop , che aveva offerto 56 miliardi di dollari, quattro volte il proprio valore. Nella presentazione dei risultati del primo e del secondo trimestre di quest’anno, l’eliminazione dei posti di lavoro non era mai stata citata.

items.title: Un importante politico dell’Irlanda del Nord, già condannato per stupro, è accusato di aver violentato una donna nel parlamento britannico
items.content:
La Metropolitan Police, la polizia di Londra, sta indagando sull’importante politico nordirlandese Jeffrey Donaldson, accusato di aver stuprato una donna nel parlamento britannico a Westminster nel 2016. Donaldson ha 63 anni, è l’ex leader del Partito democratico unionista dell’Irlanda del Nord (DUP), di centrodestra, e la settimana scorsa era stato condannato a 15 anni di carcere per stupro e molestie sessuali contro due donne che all’epoca dei fatti (tra il 1985 e il 2008) erano minorenni.

Le nuove accuse sono state segnalate alla Metropolitan Police dalla polizia dell’Irlanda del Nord, che aveva raccolto la testimonianza della donna coinvolta, a sua volta nordirlandese. Donaldson era diventato leader del DUP nel 2021, e si era dimesso nel 2024, dopo essere stato incriminato per i reati per cui è già stato condannato.

items.title: No order, no seat: Starbucks China rolls out new store policy
items.summary: Starbucks says it is improving customers' in-store experience as it competes with homegrown rivals.
items.content:
Taking a seat at a Starbucks in China? Just make sure you're also ordering something there.

A new policy by Starbucks China takes effect across all its 8,000 stores on Thursday, making it mandatory for people to purchase items if they want to sit in its cafes.

Starbucks China said the move was part of efforts to improve the "in-store experience" for customers. The company is facing stiff competition from homegrown brands such as Luckin Coffee.

Starbucks stores around the world have also been wrestling with non-paying seat-hoggers and other undesirable behaviour from customers.

In South Korea, Starbucks has told customers to stop bringing "bulky items" into their stores , after some patrons reportedly hogged seats with printers and desktop computers in tow.

In North America, Starbucks reversed its open-door policy which for years allowed people to use their seats and toilets without buying anything, saying that it wanted to "prioritise" paying customers.

Ahead of the official announcement on Wednesday, reports of the new seating policy at China's Starbucks stores had been circulating this week - along with social media videos of what appear to be "purchase to sit" signs in Starbucks stores.

"Finally, there won't be peak periods where people are just sitting there not ordering anything, drinking Luckin coffee, playing games and yelling on the phone," reads one of the top-liked comment on Weibo. "Every time I walk around, there's nowhere to sit,"

"There's nothing wrong with it. I'd feel awkward sitting there if I didn't make a purchase. I'd rather leave the seats for those who made purchases and need the seats," another Weibo user commented.

Last month, a Starbucks store in Sichuan province sparked debate after video of its chained-up outdoor seats and tables were circulated on social media. It appeared to be an attempt to block people from sitting there without paying.

Since opening its first store there in 1999, China has become Starbucks' second-largest market. But it has faced stiff competition in recent years from Luckin and other local brands that offer cheaper products.

Luckin also offers a robust app-based ordering system that prioritises grab-and-go transactions, challenging Starbucks' model of a full cafe experience where people can sit down and enjoy their food and drinks.

In 2023, Luckin overtook Starbucks as China's largest coffee chain.

Starbucks said last year it would sell 60% stake of its business in China as part of a $4bn (£3.04bn) deal with investment firm Boyu Capital.

In another statement on Wednesday, Starbucks China said it was planning to increase staffing and improve digital systems at its stores, among other investments to "ensure customers receive timely and warm service even during peak hours".

items.title: US embassy accuses Canada of election meddling ahead of midterms
items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the claim, noting that US initiated trade actions against Canada.
items.content:
The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms.

The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".

Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during the second Trump administration.

The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".

It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.

For example, it says that when Industry Minister Mélanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates."

Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support".

Asked on Wednesday about the allegations, Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada.

"We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.

He said his government's response has been "in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy".

Carney, who was announcing a nearly C$9bn ($6.2bn) aid package in response to US tariffs, was accompanied by both Joly and Ford.

Ford said that he has "no interest at all" in interfering in US elections.

"I'll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability," Ford said, adding that he will focus on Ontario and Canada.

"The people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms," he said.

Last week, Minister Joly denied Canadian interference and said that Canadians "never accept that also being done to us in Canada", according to CBC.

She said that her recent visits to the US were "to attract investments" from American companies, which she plans to continue.

Washington and Ottawa have argued for months over tariffs and trade , which once flowed freely across their borders, and the effects of Canada's counter measures.

Earlier this month, US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned that US officials are "closely watching" Canada's politicians for signs of election interference.

Trump administration officials have also been accused of making inappropriate remarks about the separation referendum in the province of Alberta this week.

A petition calling for Hoekstra's removal from his post for "undermining the Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations" has received more than 280,000 signatures.

'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism

items.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.summary: Article URL: https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50190363 Points: 420 # Comments: 131
items.content:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videos

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.

Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.

That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.

I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.

The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one.

The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.

I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.

I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage.

I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.

Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves.

In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.

To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations. 2

The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.

There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.

For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.

Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.

About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.

Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.

In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.

I use three tests. ShellBench has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. PresetBench has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.

The memory test has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training. 3

The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.

It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after echo green >> colors , running cat colors often doesn't show the appended line.

For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.

But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen ( vim test.txt , man , clear ) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.

What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.

That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.

The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.

This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.

This might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to vim opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.

Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.

items.title: Come scegliere il caricatore USB-C giusto (eh no, non sono tutti uguali)
items.summary: Scegliere un caricatore? Semplice, alla fine hanno tutti lo stesso connettore USB-C. Peccato che non sia così: cavi diversi, sigle diverse, potenze diverse ma alimentatori esteriormente molto simili tra loro: la scelta di un caricatore non è sempre facile. Perché se è vero che oggi con un solo alimentatore si può caricare di tutto, è anche vero che deve essere scelto bene. ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Alzi la mano chi non ha in casa un cassetto pieno di cavi ingarbugliati e di caricatori. Un alimentatore per il telefono, uno per il notebook, uno per il tablet, ognuno con la sua spina e, nel caso di prodotti meno recenti, anche con un connettore proprietario. Oggi, per fortuna, il cassetto si sta progressivamente svuotando grazie all'unione di due tasselli: da un lato lo standard USB-C Power Delivery, che permette a un solo alimentatore di erogare potenze diverse a seconda del dispositivo collegato, e dall'altro la normativa europea che ha spinto tutti i produttori ad abbandonare i connettori proprietari in favore dell'USB-C come connettore universale.

Il risultato è da un lato che oggi insieme agli apparecchi quasi sempre non viene più incluso l'alimentatore; ma dall'altro lato è vero che, nella maggior parte dei casi, un unico caricatore può bastare per smartphone, tablet, cuffie, console portatili e persino per il notebook (sempre che questo non sia un laptop da gaming che ha richieste particolari in termini di potenza).

Nonostante questo, scegliere un alimentatore non è semplicissimo, anche se dovrebbe esserlo: il fatto che il connettore USB-C si infili nell'alimentatore non basta a garantire una ricarica veloce, o addirittura la ricarica nel caso di dispositivi energivori. Questa guida, realizzata in collaborazione con Techly , è pensata per spiegare, dalla A alla Z, tutto quello che c'è da sapere per scegliere il caricatore perfetto.

La sigla USB-C indica semplicemente la forma di quel connettore, che ormai dovrebbe essere familiare, ovale e utilizzabile da entrambi i lati. Power Delivery, spesso abbreviato in PD, è invece il protocollo che regola quanta energia viene trasferita attraverso quel connettore: il caricatore non eroga indistintamente la stessa potenza a tutti i dispositivi, ma comunica con l’apparecchio collegato e regola automaticamente l’energia in uscita, assicurando la massima velocità di ricarica compatibile con entrambi. Un alimentatore Power Delivery negozia con il dispositivo collegato una serie di profili di tensione, solitamente 5, 9, 12, 15 o 20 Volt, scegliendo quello più adatto per ricaricare un prodotto al meglio. Per questo la prima cosa da cercare quando si sceglie un caricatore non è solo la porta USB-C, quella ormai ce l'hanno tutti, ma la dicitura specifica USB-C PD 3.2 (l'ultima versione dello standard), che è quella che garantisce la compatibilità con il più ampio numero di dispositivi possibili. Un laptop, ad esempio, ha bisogno di 20 Volt, che un alimentatore da smartphone classico non può erogare, mentre la Nintendo Switch, tanto per fare un esempio, ha bisogno di 15 Volt.

La seconda domanda che solitamente una persona si fa è: "Quanti Watt mi servono?". Sebbene la tentazione sia quella di prendere sempre l'alimentatore con il numero più alto disponibile, è probabilmente più indicato ragionare per fasce e secondo le necessità, perché a potenza più elevata corrisponde un caricatore non solo più costoso ma anche più pesante e ingombrante.

Esiste tuttavia un modo per avere un caricatore che sia potente ma al tempo stesso compatto: basta scegliere un caricatore GaN . Sostituendo il silicio con il nitruro di gallio (GaN) nei componenti interni, materiale che permette di gestire le stesse potenze con meno dispersione di calore e quindi con dimensioni molto più contenute, le aziende sono riuscite a costruire caricatori per laptop piccoli come quelli tradizionali per smartphone. Il che da un lato è un evidente vantaggio, ma dall'altro può ingenerare ulteriore confusione: la dimensione dell'alimentatore non può essere presa più come "metro" della sua potenza.

L' IPW-PD65W , ad esempio, è un alimentatore da 65 Watt che pesa poco e sta tranquillamente in tasca. I modelli GaN sono leggermente più costosi, ma valgono la spesa.

Questo è, per esempio, un caricatore da 20 W (esiste anche in versione da 30 W) adatto per smartphone e piccoli dispositivi.

Questo alimentatore dispone di due porte, una USB-C e una USB-A così da essere adatto a qualsiasi cavo e distribuisce la sua potenza sulle due porte.

Collegando solo un device, tutta la potenza verrà destinata a quell'apparecchio, secondo le combinazioni di tensioni e potenze scritte sull'alimentatore.

Salendo a 30 W, come con questo alimentatore , che è anche GaN, si guadagna un po' di margine anche su tablet più esigenti e alcuni notebook ultraleggeri.

La tecnologia GaN permette comunque di mantenere le dimensioni compatte, rendendolo un apparecchio adatto anche per i viaggi. Non a caso si tratta di un vero "best seller" del sito Techly, anche in considerazione del costo contenuto.

L'erogazione di potenza massima è 30W, disponibili (una per volta) su entrambe le porte, anche quella USB-A. Nel caso di utilizzo contemporaneo di entrambe le uscite, cosa comunque possibile, la potenza su ogni porta si dimezza.

La soglia dei 45 W è quella che comincia a coprire i notebook più sottili, anche se con qualche compromesso nei carichi di lavoro intensi, mentre il vero salto arriva a 65 W, la potenza che oggi rappresenta il taglio più versatile in assoluto: come vedremo, riesce a ricaricare praticamente ogni dispositivo di uso quotidiano, incluso un MacBook Air o la maggior parte degli ultrabook Windows.

Questo modello (disponibile anche nella variante da 45 W) ha una sola uscita USB-C ma è stupefacente per dimensioni contenute e efficienza, tanto che, anche durante la ricarica, si scalda molto poco.

Si arriva infine a 100 W (o superiori), necessari solo per workstation portatili o per chi vuole ricaricare rapidamente due dispositivi impegnativi contemporaneamente dalla stessa presa, perché, come abbiamo detto, la potenza indicata per i caricatori con più prese USB-C è quella aggregata e non quella erogabile dalla singola presa.

Il modello IPW-PD100W-2A2CW, per esempio, è un GaN da 100 W e dispone di 4 porte di uscita, due USB-C e due USB-A.

Ma attenzione, in questo caso (è ben specificato nei dettagli tecnici) collegando un solo device alla prima porta USB-C è possibile ottenere tutti i 100W con una connessione a 20V e 5 A, per esempio per caricare un MacBook Pro o una workstation potente; se invece si attaccano più device insieme, la potenza si distribuisce secondo alcuni schemi: per esempio 65 + 20 W sulle due porte USB-C; o 65 + 18 sulle due USB-A.

Chi vuole il massimo della versatilità, invece, sempre rimanendo sui modelli "a muro", può trovare la propria soluzione nel caricatore IPW-PD140W-WH da 140 W.

Le porte sono quattro, tre USB-C e una USB-A, mix che rispecchia meglio la natura dei device attuali.

Collegando un solo PC alla USB-C, si erogano appunto fino a 140W secondo gli standard Power Delivery.

Ma anche collegando, per esempio, due MacBook Air, si ottengono 65 W ciascuno, quanto basta per alimentarli entrambi.

Oppure si possono fare altri mix usando tutte le quattro porte, che consentono di alimentare e caricare per esempio un PC, un tablet, uno smartphone e uno smartwatch, tutto con dimensioni e pesi molto contenuti.

Ne giova anche l'ordine di casa: niente ciabatte e niente diversi caricabatterie.

Spesso si pensa che sia solo l'alimentatore a decidere quanta potenza deve arrivare al dispositivo, ma non è così: anche il cavo ha un limite di potenza che può trasportare. Correnti elevate, infatti, porterebbero i cavi più sottili a scaldarsi, quindi con alcuni cavi le potenze vengono limitate in automatico. È questo il motivo per il quale molti smartphone con sistemi di ricarica veloce, anche 120 Watt, vengono venduti con il loro cavo (e richiedono il loro caricatore): certe tecnologie di ricarica proprietarie richiedono la corretta combinazione di cavo e alimentatore. Non tutti i cavi, infatti, sono progettati per reggere i 240 Watt massimi che l'USB-C supporta: molti dei cavi "semplici" in circolazione si fermano a 60 W, e alcuni addirittura a potenze inferiori, anche se il connettore è identico e sembra funzionare normalmente. Il risultato, nel migliore dei casi, è una ricarica più lenta di quanto il caricatore potrebbe offrire; nel peggiore, un cavo non certificato di provenienza dubbia può scaldarsi eccessivamente sotto carico prolungato.

Come fa un cavo a ridurre la potenza del caricatore? I cavi USB-C più evoluti integrano un piccolo chip chiamato e-marker, che comunica al caricatore le caratteristiche reali del cavo, dalla potenza massima alla velocità dati. Per chi ha un Mac, esiste WhatCable, un'applicazione gratuita e open source che legge questi dati e segnala in modo chiaro se un cavo sta "limitando" la ricarica rispetto a quanto il caricatore potrebbe erogare. Se avete nel cassetto un po' di cavi, WhatCable può essere utile per etichettarli: "smartphone", "tablet", "pc" e così via.

Sul sito Techly, nella descrizione dei tantissimi cavi USB-C disponibili (tutti rigorosamente a norma), è chiaramente indicata la potenza di ricarica gestita.

Il codice ICOC MU4-40G240W1 , per esempio, è uno dei più completi e, non solo è in grado di trasferire dati fino a 40 Gbps, ma gestisce ricariche secondo lo standard Power Delivery 3.1 fino a 240 W di potenza. Praticamente ci fai tutto.

items.title: iRobot è così sicura dei suoi Roomba da farteli provare a casa per 30 giorni
items.summary: Il Roomba si porta a casa, si mette al lavoro sui propri pavimenti e, se non convince, si restituisce entro 30 giorni con il rimborso del prezzo pagato. Vale anche sui modelli in offerta ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Un robot aspirapolvere si sceglie leggendo le schede, ma si giudica solo a casa propria, tra il divano e il tappeto del soggiorno. Per questo iRobot ha deciso di togliere di mezzo il dubbio. Chi compra un Roomba ha 30 giorni per provarlo nella vita di tutti i giorni e, se non lo convince, lo restituisce e riceve indietro i soldi. Il programma si chiama Soddisfatti o Rimborsati e sarà attivo fino al 31 marzo 2027 .

Dietro c'è un ragionamento semplice. Un'azienda propone una prova così lunga solo quando è convinta che, dopo un mese di pulizie, il robot si sarà guadagnato il suo posto in casa.

Passerà sotto il letto? E sul tappeto a pelo lungo si arrampicherà o rimarrà impigliato? Riuscirà a stare dietro al pelo del gatto che cambia stagione? Come laverà il mio parquet? Sono le domande che si fa chiunque stia per comprare un robot , e nessuna scheda tecnica può rispondere per una casa che non conosce.

Trenta giorni bastano per scoprirlo . In pochissimo tempo un Roomba impara la pianta dell'appartamento e si abitua a soglie e bordi dei tappeti, passando dal parquet del soggiorno alle piastrelle del bagno. Chi ha animali lo vede al lavoro nei giorni normali, quelli in cui il pelo si accumula negli angoli e sotto i mobili. E chi vuole avere sempre un pavimento lavato di fresco potrà testare anche le capacità di lavare e asciugare il rullo del robot sulla base AutoWash dei modelli che la prevedono, per evitare muffe e cattivi odori.

È anche il modo migliore per apprezzare i Roomba più recenti . Il 115 e i Plus 415, 515 e 575 hanno un profilo fino al 21% più sottile del Roomba Plus 505. Se sulla carta è un numero, sotto il proprio divano diventa la polvere che finalmente sparisce.

Il meccanismo è pensato per non complicare la vita a chi compra.

1. Si acquista il Roomba da un qualunque rivenditore, in negozio oppure online.

2. Entro 10 giorni dall'acquisto lo si registra su irobot.it , caricando lo scontrino o la conferma d'ordine.

3. Si usa il robot in casa , come si farebbe con qualunque elettrodomestico appena comprato.

4. Se non convince, entro 30 giorni dall'acquisto si chiede il reso dalla propria area riservata . Un corriere passa a ritirarlo senza costi e il prezzo pagato torna con un bonifico.

L'unica accortezza è conservare la scatola originale e lo scontrino , perché il Roomba torna indietro completo, come è arrivato.

La prova vale anche quando il Roomba si compra in promozione. Chi approfitta di uno sconto da un rivenditore conserva i suoi 30 giorni e, in caso di reso, riceve indietro quanto ha effettivamente pagato. Restano fuori soltanto i Roomba ottenuti come omaggio, per esempio in un'offerta 3x2, o vinti come premio di un concorso.

Con le offerte di ottobre ancora in corso , è il momento più conveniente per mettere un Roomba alla prova .

Sul negozio ufficiale di iRobot i 30 giorni ci sono già "di serie", per ogni acquisto . Chi ordina da irobot.it non deve registrarsi al programma. Se il robot non lo convince, lo restituisce con la normale procedura di reso del sito, entro 30 giorni dalla consegna.

Il programma non si limita a qualche modello di punta. Comprende i Roomba d'ingresso come il 115 , i Plus delle serie 400, 500 e 600, i Max delle serie 700 e 800, fino al Mini Combo. Valgono anche le versioni proposte su Amazon. L'unica condizione è che il robot sia nuovo e distribuito in Italia da Nital, con il Sigillo di Garanzia Ufficiale Italia sulla confezione.

Se ci si vuole affidare a punti vendita fisici, il rivenditore più vicino si trova con la ricerca dei rivenditori di iRobot , mentre la pagina del programma spiega come registrarsi . Per l'elenco completo dei modelli e tutte le condizioni del rimborso conviene leggere il regolamento .
